young.html: In the last part of his poem, the Paradiso, Dante flies up into the sky with Beatrice. He does not need a rocket. He looks at Beatrice, Beatrice looks up at the light of heaven, and they rise, faster than lightning, from one sphere to the next.

In Dante's time people pictured the sky as a set of giant, clear spheres nested one inside another, with the Earth at the center. Each sphere carried a shining body: the Moon, then Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, then all the fixed stars. Beyond those spun one more sphere that turned all the rest, and beyond everything was the home of God, full of light.

young.name: gb-dante-cosmos
young.cap: Climb through the heavens from the Moon to the Empyrean. Tap a sphere to read who Dante meets there.

young.html: In each heaven Dante meets happy souls who shine like lights. In the heaven of the Sun he meets wise teachers, including Thomas Aquinas, dancing in rings of light. Everything gets brighter as he goes, and Beatrice's smile gets so bright he can hardly look at it. At the very end Dante sees God, and the poem stops, because, he says, there are no words for what he saw.

Make the spheres. Cut ten circles of paper, each a little bigger than the last, or stack ten bowls inside one another. Put a small ball or bead in the middle for the Earth. Label each circle: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Fixed stars, Primum Mobile, Empyrean. How is this picture different from what we know about the solar system today?

full.html: Paradiso, the last 33 cantos of the Comedy, follows Dante and Beatrice from the top of Mount Purgatory through the heavens to God. It is the hardest canticle to read and, for many readers, the most beautiful. Where Hell was a funnel of darkness, Paradise is made of light, music and motion.

full.text:
His glory, by whose might all things are mov'd,
Pierces the universe, and in one part
Sheds more resplendence, elsewhere less. ...
full.author: Dante

full.html: Dante's cosmos is the one taught from Aristotle and Ptolemy: a round Earth at the center, surrounded by turning spheres. The Moon and the Sun counted as "planets," wanderers among the stars, so there were seven planetary spheres, then the sphere of the fixed stars, then the Primum Mobile ("first moved"), which turns all the others. Beyond them, outside space and time, is the Empyrean, God's heaven.

full.name: gb-dante-cosmos
full.cap: The ten heavens of the Paradiso, with our own summaries of what happens in each.

full.title: Counting the heavens
full.q: How many moving spheres are there in Dante's heavens, and how many heavens in all?
steps: Seven planets (Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn): 7 spheres.
Add the fixed stars and the Primum Mobile: $7 + 2 = 9$ moving spheres.
Add the Empyrean, which does not move: $9 + 1 = 10$.
full.a: Nine moving spheres, ten heavens in all. Nine, three times three, mattered to Dante, as it did in his early book about Beatrice.

full.html: In Canto II Beatrice explains the dark marks on the Moon, and she proposes an experiment: set up three mirrors at different distances, put a light behind you, and see that the far mirror shines as brightly as the near ones, only smaller. It is one of the first descriptions of an experiment in a great poem, though her explanation of the marks is not ours.

full.text: Why the blessed appear in different heavens

full.html: In the Moon, Dante meets Piccarda, a woman who could not keep her vows. He asks if she wishes for a higher place. She answers that the blessed want only what God wills.

full.text:
E'en as our King, who in us plants his will;
And in his will is our tranquillity;
It is the mighty ocean, whither tends
Whatever it creates and nature makes.
full.author: Dante

full.html: Beatrice then explains (Canto IV) that all the blessed really live together in the Empyrean. They appear in the lower spheres only to show Dante, in a way a human mind can grasp, that they share in heaven's joy in different degrees, and each is content.

items: The Sun (Cantos X to XIV): twelve wise souls form a ring of light around Dante and Beatrice, then a second ring. Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican, tells the life of Saint Francis, and the Franciscan Bonaventure tells the life of Saint Dominic. Each praises the other's founder.
Mars (Cantos XIV to XVIII): Dante's ancestor Cacciaguida tells him he will be exiled, will learn how bitter another man's bread tastes, and must still write everything he has seen.
Jupiter (Cantos XVIII to XX): the souls of just rulers form the shape of an eagle, which speaks with one voice about divine justice.
The fixed stars (Cantos XXII to XXVII): Dante looks down and sees the Earth, so small it makes him smile. Saint Peter examines him on faith, Saint James on hope and Saint John on love.
The Primum Mobile (Cantos XXVII to XXIX): God appears as a single point of intense light, circled by nine rings of angels.
The Empyrean (Cantos XXX to XXXIII): the blessed sit in a vast white rose. Beatrice takes her place in it, and Saint Bernard becomes Dante's last guide.

full.html: Bernard prays to Mary for Dante, and Dante is allowed to look into the light of God. He sees three circles of one light, and within them a human likeness, and he struggles to understand how they fit, until a flash of understanding comes. His power to imagine fails, but his will and desire now turn in harmony with God.

full.text:
Here vigour fail'd the tow'ring fantasy:
But yet the will roll'd onward, like a wheel
In even motion, by the Love impell'd,
That moves the sun in heav'n and all the stars.
full.work: Paradiso, Canto XXXIII (the last lines of the Comedy)
full.author: Dante

full.html: Thinking Dante believed heaven is "up in the sky" like a place you could reach by flying. The poem says itself that the spheres are shown to Dante as a picture for the human mind. The Empyrean is beyond space altogether.

deep.text: Light and the limits of language

deep.html: Again and again in the Paradiso Dante says that memory and words fail him. That is not a weakness of the poem but its subject: how can anyone describe what is greater than the mind? Dante answers with images of light, music, circles and a rose, and with Beatrice's growing beauty, which he can describe only by saying he cannot.

Dante's heavens are a medieval picture that later science replaced. Copernicus, Kepler and Galileo, later on this ladder, put the Sun at the center and showed that the heavens are made of the same kind of stuff as the Earth. Galileo himself, as a young man, gave lectures in Florence on the shape and size of Dante's Inferno. The poem's picture of the cosmos is gone, but readers still find in it a vision of an ordered, meaningful universe.

items: Piccarda is content with a lower place. Is it possible to be completely happy without having the most?
Why does Dante need a different guide for each part of the journey: Virgil, then Beatrice, then Bernard?
If words fail, why write at all? What else can a poet do?
Dante saw the Earth from the stars and smiled at how small it was. How might seeing your life "from above" change it?

deep.html: Compare Ptolemy's Almagest and Aristotle's On the Heavens for Dante's cosmos, Aquinas for his theology, and Milton for another poem of heaven.

questions: Dante rises by looking at Beatrice, who looks at God. Who helps you "rise" when you are learning something?
Piccarda says "in his will is our tranquillity." What do you think she means?
What is the most beautiful light you have ever seen? Could you describe it to someone who wasn't there?
Dante ends with "the Love ... that moves the sun ... and all the stars." Why might he end a long poem with love?
How is Dante's picture of the sky different from ours? What would he find most surprising about what we know now?
care: This rung presents Dante's Christian vision of heaven as his own, without arguing for or against it.
